items.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 29, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Lester Young composed a melody over ‘I Got Rhythm’ and he called it ‘Lester Leaps In.’

ctx.x: Oh, big ones man. The one that I can think of offhand that comes to me, it’s funny and it was a real learning experience for me. I got put with a quartet. Piano, bass, drums and an alto player, to do a festival. An indoor festival. And everything was going fine. We were about 3/4 of the way through the set. And it’s like this it’s bass, drums, alto, piano. And I turned to the band and I say, “rhythm changes in E flat.” Then I turned to the audience

and say, “George and Ira Gershwin wrote a song called ‘I Got Rhythm.’ Lester Young composed a melody over ‘I Got Rhythm’ and he called it ‘Lester Leaps In.’ The lyrical version is called ‘I Got the Blues.’” I turned to the band and say, “one/two/one-two-three- four.” Now maybe they weren’t listening. But the bass player — you know where this is going already, right? The bass player and the drummer start to play rhythm changes. And the piano player and the alto player are playing the blues. Now that works for…

items.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, November 11, 2017 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Well I’m a fan of Lester Young and his lingo, and Lenny Bruce, and Lord Buckley, and all those hipsters.

ctx.x: I like the fact that in your vocabulary you still have the words “it’s a gas” “solid” that kind of stuff.

Well I’m a fan of Lester Young and his lingo, and Lenny Bruce, and Lord Buckley, and all those hipsters. They were, to me, they were funny and bright and articulate and they said a lot with a little. You know?

When you were scatting last night on “Four” I took note of the one note that you held for like four bars. I think it was the last four bars of the form. You found that note, which fit every chord, and the fact that you heard that I thought was informative.
